archetype.name: Pocket Passer (scramble-capable)
archetype.definition: A big-armed, 6-6 pocket thrower who has always won from the pocket first, but who now leans more and more on his legs to escape a collapsing protection and a run-first plan that gives him little to work with.

report.headline: A good quarterback trapped in a broken offense, and paying for it in sacks and interceptions
report.take:
Herbert's 2026 reads like a collapse: -0.188 EPA per dropback (45th of 54), an 11.5% sack rate (48th), 11 interceptions (52nd), and a team that didn't win until Week 10. His career says otherwise. He posted positive EPA per play in all six prior seasons, peaking at 0.199 in 2021, and his charted bad-throw rate this year (12.6%, 10th of 42) is almost identical to last year's 13.3%. The arm and the ball placement are largely still there. What has fallen apart is everything around them.

The environment is about as hostile as it gets. The Chargers rank 32nd in offensive EPA, 32nd in success rate, and dead last in pass rate over expected at -10.2. Harbaugh's offense is running into a wall at 30th in rush EPA rather than setting anything up. The line allows a hit on 19.8% of dropbacks (31st), and he is hit or sacked on 22.1% of his. The run-heavy calls leave him in obvious passing downs: his third downs come at an average of 8.7 yards to go, and he converts a third of them. One-score fourth quarters have been a disaster: -0.831 EPA per play with 10 sacks on 33 snaps. His pass-catchers split cleanly. Harris, Johnston and McConkey are all above +0.22 EPA per target, while the two tight ends, Gadsden and Kolar, are deeply negative on 54 combined looks.

What the numbers hide is that not all of this is on the line. His pressure-to-sack rate has climbed for years: 17.1% as a rookie, around 30% the last two seasons, and 40.8% now. He has always held the ball and hunted for something better, and behind this front that habit gets punished. The interceptions are also concentrated rather than random. Nine of the 11 have come on throws of 10+ air yards, five of them on just 59 intermediate attempts with an -8.5 CPOE. The deep ball still nets positive EPA (+0.13 per attempt) despite four picks on 29 throws. It looks like a quarterback forcing windows because the short game gives him nothing. His 58 throws behind the line are at -0.245 EPA per attempt, so the screen game is bleeding drives.

The last three games show a quarterback adjusting. His CPOE is +4.5 over his season mark, and both completion rate and yards per attempt are up, but the staff is getting there by shrinking him. In Week 8 he threw at 3.1% aggressiveness with a 5.0-yard intended air distance. The sack rate in that stretch got worse, to 14.1%, so efficiency hasn't actually moved. Expect a quarterback who is better than his rate stats and who will look better as the interception luck evens out. He still can't produce top-end passing numbers in this system and behind this line.

strengths.title: Ball placement hasn't gone anywhere
strengths.body: His charted bad-throw rate ranks 10th of 42 and sits right in line with his career norms. The negative CPOE is concentrated in the intermediate area and the screen game, not spread across his whole tree. The recent stretch backs it up: CPOE over the last three games is well above his season figure. That should hold, because accuracy has been stable for him across six seasons.

strengths.title: Legs as a pressure valve
strengths.body: He ranks 4th among quarterbacks in rushing yards, and his scrambles return positive EPA (+0.092 per scramble) on nearly a tenth of his dropbacks. This isn't a fluke. He finished 2nd in rushing yards last season, so the running is a real part of his game now rather than garbage-time padding. It also keeps his weekly floor afloat when the passing goes nowhere, as in the Week 10 win.

strengths.title: Wide receivers still produce
strengths.body: Harris, Johnston and McConkey all clear +0.22 EPA per target. When he gets the ball outside to his receivers, the offense works, and throws to the left side are a positive +11.4 EPA in total. The problem is distribution and protection, not his connection with the wideouts.

concerns.title: Sacks: a bad line meets an old habit
concerns.body: An 11.5% sack rate (48th) is partly structural: the offense ranks 31st in hit rate allowed. Part of it is him, though. His pressure-to-sack rate has risen nearly every season, from 17.1% as a rookie to 40.8% now, a sign of a quarterback who extends plays looking for the big answer. With a starting-caliber tackle like Pipkins on IR, expect this to stay ugly. It is the single biggest drag on his EPA.

concerns.title: Interceptions downfield, especially intermediate
concerns.body: Nine of his 11 interceptions came on throws of 10+ air yards, five of them in the 10-19 range, where his CPOE is -8.5. Some of that is forcing throws when the run game and screens leave him behind the sticks. Some is small-sample bad luck: four deep picks on 29 attempts is extreme. He threw 13 picks last year too, so a few turnovers are part of his game, but the current 4.3% rate should drift down.

concerns.title: Close-game fourth quarters and the right side
concerns.body: In one-score fourth quarters he is at -0.831 EPA per play, with 10 sacks on 33 plays. Throws to his right are a -24.5 EPA hole. Both point to the same thing: when the defense knows he has to pass, this line and this route tree don't hold up. That is fixable only with better protection, not with anything he does alone.

trend.note: Completion rate and CPOE have climbed over the last three games as the staff shortened his throws. The sack rate rose with them, so EPA per dropback hasn't moved off its poor season level. The Week 10 win came on just 18 attempts, with his legs doing much of the work.

nextGame.headline: Jets' soft short-area defense fits the quick game he's using now
nextGame.body:
This is the right defense for the version of Herbert the Chargers have been running lately. The Jets rank 29th in pass EPA allowed and 31st in success rate, and they are 31st against short passes. That is exactly where his offense has been failing and where the staff has been steering him. They've given up 2.1 passing TDs per game to quarterbacks (26th). Their low yardage allowed mostly reflects opponents running on them; the per-play numbers are bad. They also leak production to tight ends, so even his weakest target group has room. The caveat is the pass rush: the Jets' sack rate ranks 12th, and a sack-prone quarterback behind a 31st-ranked hit-rate line can still stall drives. At home indoors as 3-point favorites with a 40.5 total, the Book expects a low-scoring game the Chargers control, which in this offense means a lot of running and modest volume.

On availability, McConkey (back spasms) missed Week 10 and Brenen Thompson (hamstring) was also inactive. McConkey is his most efficient target, and his return would matter more than anything else on the Chargers' side. Pipkins remains on IR, so the tackle depth stays thin. The site lists Herbert himself as questionable, though the dossier carries no injury note; his snap share dipped to 79% in Week 9, so check his status. For the Jets, corner Jarvis Brownlee Jr. is out, which thins a secondary that is already struggling. Geno Smith is questionable with an ankle. If he sits, the Chargers are more likely to play from ahead, which in Harbaugh's offense lowers Herbert's attempt count rather than raising it.

keyMatchups.title: Short passing game vs 31st-ranked short defense
keyMatchups.body: His throws under 10 air yards have cost a combined -16.7 EPA, and screens behind the line have been the worst of it. The Jets allow +0.205 EPA on short passes, 31st in the league. If the quick game is ever going to work, it's here.

keyMatchups.title: Tight ends get a soft draw
keyMatchups.body: Gadsden and Kolar have been drags on the offense, but the Jets allow 0.39 EPA per play to TE1s (25th) and see an above-league share of targets go to tight ends. A friendly matchup for his weakest group could turn some dead targets into gains.

keyMatchups.title: Jets pass rush vs a sack-prone pocket
keyMatchups.body: The Jets' 6.9% sack rate is 12th, solid if not dominant. Against a quarterback taking sacks on 40.8% of his pressures, a decent rush still decides drives. Getting the ball out quickly decides whether the soft coverage gets exploited.

nextGame.watch: Whether McConkey is back and whether Herbert can stay under three sacks; if both happen, this is his best passing day in weeks.

restOfSeason.body:
The bottom line is a quarterback who is better than his rate stats, stuck in a role that caps him. The interception rate should come down: 4.3% is well above almost every season of his career, and the deep picks are a small-sample spike. His accuracy has already started recovering. The sacks will not fix themselves. The protection is bottom-two, the tackle depth is hurt, and his own sack tendency has been rising for three years. Harbaugh's league-low pass rate over expected means volume stays low, so even a good week looks like 220 yards rather than 300.

Expect something like 175-225 passing yards a game, with touchdown passes improving toward one a game as the red-zone results (5 TDs, 0 INTs there) pull his 2.4% TD rate up a bit. Expect 20-35 rushing yards to keep giving him a floor. The upside case needs McConkey healthy and some help at tackle; without them, he settles in as a below-average passer whose legs keep him usable.
swingFactors: Pass protection and Pipkins' return from IR
Whether the staff lets him throw more on early downs

confidence.note: Nine games and a clear career baseline, but protection and receiver health are shifting.
